desc:
A railway station timetable is given by two arrays of the same length: train i arrives at time arrivals[i] and leaves at time departures[i], with arrivals[i] ≤ departures[i]. Times are whole minutes and the trains are listed in no particular order.

After a train leaves, its platform must be cleaned for gap more minutes. So a train occupies its platform for the whole closed interval [arrival, departure + gap], and the platform can be given to another train only from time departure + gap + 1 on. In particular, with gap = 0 a train arriving at the very minute another one leaves still needs a different platform.

Return the minimum number of platforms that lets every train stop without waiting.

arrivals = [900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800], departures = [910, 1200, 1120, 1130, 1900, 2000], gap = 0  ->  3

arrivals = [1, 20], departures = [5, 25], gap = 10  ->  1
arrivals = [1, 20], departures = [5, 25], gap = 15  ->  2

In the first example three trains are in the station at time 1100. In the last two, the first train blocks its platform until minute 15 (gap 10) or minute 20 (gap 15), and the second train arrives at minute 20: it fits only in the first case.
hints: The answer equals the largest number of trains that need a platform at the same moment, where a train needs it until departure + gap.
That maximum can only increase at an arrival time. Look at the arrivals and the (shifted) release times separately, each in increasing order, instead of at the pairs.

Sort the arrivals and the values departure + gap. Walk through the arrivals with a pointer into the release times: if the next arrival is at or before the earliest unreleased platform, a new platform is needed; otherwise a platform is released.
editorial: Replace every departure by the time its platform becomes available again, departure + gap; the platform is busy on the closed interval [arrival, departure + gap]. Sort the arrival times and these release times independently; the pairing between them does not matter for counting how many platforms are busy at a moment. Use two pointers i (arrivals) and j (releases) and a counter cur of busy platforms. If arrivals[i] ≤ release[j], the next event is an arrival (a tie goes to the arrival because the platform is still busy at that minute): increment cur, record the maximum and advance i. Otherwise a platform became free strictly before the next arrival: decrement cur and advance j.

The maximum value of cur is the number of platforms needed, because intervals on a line can always be coloured with as many colours as the maximum overlap. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the sorted copies.
solution:
def minPlatforms(arrivals, departures, gap):
    arr = sorted(arrivals)
    rel = sorted(d + gap for d in departures)
    n = len(arr)
    i = j = cur = best = 0
    while i < n:
        if arr[i] <= rel[j]:
            cur += 1
            best = max(best, cur)
            i += 1
        else:
            cur -= 1
            j += 1
    return best
